standard.title: Manage digital footprint data
standard.description: Investigate and manage the digital footprint existing systems and student solutions collect and assess if the data is essential to their purpose
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain how their digital footprint is created and permanent, and consider privacy when collecting user data (AC9TDI6P10). They understand that a footprint exists but have not yet investigated what specific data systems collect, assessed whether that data is essential, or managed their own footprint settings.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate what digital footprint data existing systems and student solutions collect, manage their own footprint by reviewing privacy settings, and assess whether the data collected is essential to the system's purpose.

nodes.label: What data systems collect
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate what digital footprint data a system collects about its users
nodes.minimum_width: Given a platform or app, identify at least three types of data it collects about users (e.g. location, browsing history, contacts, usage patterns)
nodes.typical_width: Research a platform's privacy policy to identify what data is collected, how it is used, and how long it is stored; compare data collection across two platforms
wider: Investigate how recommendation algorithms used in music or video streaming services rely on tracking user habits to generate personalised content
Research how data collection practices differ between platforms marketed to young people vs adults

response_modes.reason: Investigating data collection across different platform types (social media, streaming services, youth-targeted apps) reveals that collection practices vary systematically with business model and audience. Multiple platform contexts help students see the pattern rather than treating a single platform as representative.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot name what categories of data a system collects cannot assess whether that data is essential (Node 2) or make informed decisions about privacy settings (Node 3). The investigation at Node 1 is the factual foundation for both subsequent analytical tasks.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The recommendation algorithm and youth-targeted platform directions are genuinely rich — examining how habit-tracking drives personalisation makes data collection purposeful rather than abstract, and the comparison between youth and adult platforms is analytically substantive.
success_criteria: Identifies at least three types of data a platform collects
Includes at least one type of data collected passively (not explicitly provided by the user)

nodes.label: Assessing whether data is essential
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can assess whether the data a system collects is essential to its purpose, or whether it exceeds what is needed
nodes.minimum_width: Given a system and the data it collects, identify at least one piece of data that is essential to its purpose and one that is not; explain the difference
nodes.typical_width: Assess the appropriateness of data collected by surveys or platforms — for example, identifying that providing your address is not necessary for a food preferences survey but is appropriate for a Census
wider: Evaluate whether the data collected by a student-built solution is essential — apply the same critical lens to their own design decisions
Research how the Australian Privacy Principles define data minimisation and apply this standard to a real platform

response_modes.reason: Assessing whether data is essential requires students to reason from purpose: what does this system do? → what data does it need to do that? → is this collected item necessary for that purpose? Students who cannot articulate the system's purpose cannot make the essential/non-essential distinction — they need the reasoning chain, not just the binary label.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one essential and one non-essential data item for a given system
Explains why each is or is not essential to the system's purpose

nodes.label: Managing your digital footprint
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can review and manage their own digital footprint by adjusting privacy settings and making informed decisions about data sharing
nodes.minimum_width: Review privacy settings on at least one platform they use; identify at least one setting they would change and explain why
nodes.typical_width: Review and manage privacy settings across multiple platforms; set defaults to maximum protection; explain the trade-off between functionality and privacy for specific settings
wider: Evaluate the risks of sharing personal data given that generative AI can create deepfake content from short videos and audio recordings
Investigate how privacy settings interact with recommendation systems — what changes in the user experience when data collection is restricted?

response_modes.reason: Managing footprint settings across different platforms (social media, streaming, gaming) requires students to apply the same essential/non-essential judgement in different contexts where defaults and trade-offs differ. Breadth here is breadth of platform contexts and privacy trade-off types.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The deepfake risk and recommendation system interaction directions offer advancing students a genuinely contemporary and consequential context for privacy decisions — connecting privacy settings to real risks makes the management task substantive rather than procedural.
success_criteria: Reviews privacy settings on at least one platform
Identifies at least one setting to change and explains the reasoning
